components.html:
Included in this course are 2 styles of circular tree skirts. You'll be able to choose your preferred style to knit.
Neither style is difficult to knit. With both you'll create your own personalized pattern based on the size you need.

Short Row Pinwheel Style


  • Knit in ONE PIECE - no seaming
  • Use Short Row shaping to form the sections
  • Cut 'n sew for an exact trunk opening
  • Get creative with colors swirling around the skirt.
  • Size is limited to needles available on the needlebed

Wedge Style


  • Mix and match yarn, and/or stitch pattern in each wedge
    Swatch and build the pattern for each wedge based on EACH gauge
  • No short row shaping
  • No Cut 'n Sew
  • Use sew-as you go to join wedges or neatly seam by hand
  • Choose increases or decreases to form the wedges

There are many variables when knitting (both by hand and by machine).  
  • Different colors of the SAME yarn may knit to a different gauge
  • Different dye lots of the SAME color of the SAME yarn may knit to a different gauge
  • Different models of the SAME gauge knitting machine may knit to a different gauge.
  • The SAME size knitting needle from a different manufacturer may knit to a different gauge
  • Different people, using the exactly the SAME needles, machines, and yarns may get get different gauges
SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL!
How many times have you knit something that just didn't fit?  Have you ever had colors run or fade when you washed your sweater?
So many knitting disasters can be avoided by swatching and dressing your swatch.  Machine knitters have NO EXCUSE for not swatching!  We can knit multiple swatches quickly, testing stitch patterns and tensions.  Since we don't have a lot of time invested, we can do the "throw-the-swatch-in-the-wash-with-jeans" test to see if a washable yarn will hold up.

components.html:
Instructions are for suggestions for standard gauge (mid-gauge, bulky) and for using gauge rulers.
Remember, you can knit swatches any size (as long as they are at least 5-6" square.) Be sure to be consistent and establish a template for yourself for every time you knit a swatch.

1. Cast on 60(50,30) stitches (add extra stitches so you can measure the center without edge distortion.)
  2. Knit a few rows in pattern
  3. Knit 2 rows in waste yarn (or weave a marker row)
  4. Set row counter to 000
  5. Knit the center section
    Standard gauge:
    • Knit 20 rows and knit in a yarn marker isolating the center 40 stitches
    • Knit 20 more rows and place a marker on the same needles
    • Knit 20 more rows
    Mid-Gauge:
    • Knit 10 rows and knit in a yarn marker isolating the center 30 stitches
    • Knit 10 more rows and place a marker on the same needles
    Bulky
    • Knit 15 rows and knit in a yarn marker isolating the center 40 stitches
    • Knit 15 more rows
  6. Confirm and record the total number of rows you knit for the center 60(40, 30)
  7. Knit 2 rows in waste yarn (or weave a marker row)
  8. Knit a few rows and bind off (or drop the work from the machine)
Let the swatch rest
  1. Dress the swatch as you will treat the finished item
  2. Measure the size of the 40(30, 20) stitches in the center of the swatch (between the yarn markers)
  3. Measure the size of the 60(40,30) rows between the waste yarn (or marker rows)
  4. The math
    • Divide the stitches in the middle by your measurement to get Stitches Per Inch/cm
    • Divide the rows in the middle by your measurement to get Rows Per Inch/cm
    • Multiply your stitches/rows per inch/cm times 4 to calculate stitches per 4" (10cm)

Even though we provide a tool for you to estimate the yarn needed for your skirt, understanding how to estimate yarn needed is ESSENTIAL for all of your knitting projects.
Take time to learn the basics.

components.html: For machine knitters, ravel cord is used in many situations. Let's talk a bit about ravel cord and it's uses.

Starting your knitting with waste yarn and ravel cord is a machine knitting staple technique.

Why Scrap and Ravel?

  • Use waste knitting to hang cast on comb and/or weights
  • Protect delicate/fine yarns
  • Immediately start patterning (tuck, lace, etc) with weights in place
  • Leave waste knitting in place to make blocking easier - especially for edges that roll

Scrap and Ravel Cast on

  1. Chose a yarn that is appropriate for your machine
  2. Cast on with any method
  3. Knit a few rows - end with the carriage on the left.
  4. Knit 1 row of ravel cord (smooth, slippery yarn - crochet cotton works great)
  5. Cast on over the ravel cord with your garment yarn
  6. Knit your piece
  7. After blocking, pull out the ravel cord and remove the waste yarn.


NOTE: There is no sound with the video below
Instead of using scrap yarn to cast on, consider using cast on rags and ravel cord. The rag offers a place to hang weights and can make the knitting easier.

Once you hang your cast on rag ... what's the next step?


  1. Just start knitting with your garment yarn
    Oops! How will you remove the cast on rag? What about all of those live stitches?
  2. Knit a single row of ravel cord, then start knitting with your garment yarn
    That will leave live stitches ... is that really what you want?
  3. Knit a single row of ravel cord, then create a closed cast on with your garment yarn
    For a closed finished edge for your garment, use any cast on method of your choice OVER the ravel cord.

components.html:
Practice:

  1. On the far left side of your machine cast on 5-10 stitches (any method)
  2. Knit 2 rows
  3. On the carriage side, pull one needle into working position
  4. Opposite the carriage, decrease 1 stitch
  5. Repeat until you have the length you want.
NOTE: The work will be "traveling" across the bed. If you run out of needles, move the work back to the far left side of the bed and continue knitting.

components.html:
Try your hand at Cut 'n Sew


  1. Take a swatch from a previous project or a practice swatch
  2. Mark a curved shape (1/2 or 1/4 circle)
  3. Stitch along the marking
  4. Be sure to secure the knitting well
  5. Take a deep breath and cut along the stitch line
  6. Carefully hang the edge on the machine and knit a few rows
  7. Bind off and admire your results
Want to learn more about Cut 'n Sew? Check out the Subscriber Series in the Knit it Now Library

components.html: If you plan to knit your tree skirt with wedges, the increase/decrease technique you choose is critical to the finished appearance of your skirt.
Increasing and decreasing are essential skills for machine knitters. Take time to practice different techniques.

Instruction are for standard gauge (mid/bulky gauge)
  1. Cast on 60(30) Stitches
  2. INCREASES: *Using a 2 prong transfer tool, transfer 2 stitches on each edge over 1 needle (doubling up 2 stitches) towards the center of the knitting
  3. Knit 2 rows*
  4. Repeat from * to * 6 times total
  5. Knit 4 rows
  6. DECREASES: *Using a 2 prong transfer tool, on the left side of the work, move 2 stitches one needle to the left (emptying a needle)
  7. Pick up the purl bump from the row below and fill the emptied needle (1 stitch increased)
  8. Repeat the increase on the right side of the needlebed
  9. Knit 2 rows*
  10. Repeat from * to* 6 times total
  11. Knit 2 rows
  12. Bind off

Here's a fast way to join panels as you knit. Use this technique to join the wedges of your tree skirt.
No hand seaming when you are done knitting!

Watch as we knit DECREASED wedges. This video refers to knitting a complete circle for a blanket.
Your pattern for your tree skirt leaves a hole in the center, but the knitting is exactly the same.
Also note the optional curved edge, so your skirt is rounded and not a hexagon or octagon.
Some knitters feel that decreasing is faster than increasing.
Your choice to work your wedges from the center out or from the edge in
depends on the shaping technique you use and the stitch pattern you choose to knit.

Watch as we knit INCREASED wedges. This video refers to knitting a complete circle for a blanket.
Your pattern for your tree skirt leaves a hole in the center, but the knitting is exactly the same.
Also note the optional curved edge, so your skirt is rounded and not a hexagon or octagon.
Some knitters feel that decreasing is faster than increasing.
Your choice to work your wedges from the center out or from the edge in
depends on the shaping technique you use and the stitch pattern you choose to knit.

Make your skirt special with decorative seams

  1. Right (public) side facing, hang one wedge edge
  2. e-Wrap cast on over all the needles (double or single strand of contrasting yarn)
  3. Push all strands behind the latches
  4. Wrong (private) side facing, hang the second wedge edge in the hooks of the needles
  5. Pull the strands through
  6. Loosely bind off
